video.titulo: When Cascadia Hits, This Coast Has 15 Minutes — And That's Not the Worst Part

Two tsunami evacuation towers exist in Washington. The state's own assessment says its coast needs at least 58, and possibly more than 80. Here is what the county tables actually show - and why Oregon spent the same decade moving in the opposite direction.

If you are standing in Westport when Cascadia moves, the shaking runs for minutes and the first wave arrives 10 to 15 minutes after it stops. Washington's Emergency Management Division has measured how long it takes to walk out of the inundation zone from parts of the outer coast, and in many places the answer is an hour or more. Ocosta Elementary School opened in 2016 as the first vertical evacuation structure in North America, a gym roof rated for over 1,000 people on piles driven 50 feet past the soil expected to liquefy. The Shoalwater Bay Indian Tribe dedicated the first freestanding tower at Tokeland on August fifth, 2022, and opened it to anyone in the area. A third is funded and due to break ground in Westport's Marina District at around $11.4 million, on a $16.7 million FEMA grant awarded in November 2023. Across the Columbia River, Oregon banned new schools and hospitals inside the inundation zone in 1995, then repealed that ban in 2019 with House Bill 3309. Same fault. Same wave. Opposite directions.

15:54 What You Can Actually Do About It

curva.fala: There's a stretch of the Washington coast where the math doesn't work. If you're standing in Westport when the Cascadia subduction zone finally moves, the shaking runs for several minutes. When it stops, you have somewhere

inundation zone from parts of the outer coast. In many of those areas, the answer is an hour or more on foot. Over ground that just shook for 5 minutes
with liquefied soil under you, bridges possibly gone, and everyone around you trying to do the same thing at the same moment. An hour of walking, 15 minutes of time.

That gap has already been measured and published county by county. The state has also worked out roughly how many buildings it would take to close that gap and where they need to stand. The number is somewhere between 58 and
more than 80. And only two of them exist. I'm Gwen, and this is Critical Latitude. Today, I want to walk you through the strangest hazard policy story on the West Coast,
which is that two neighboring states facing the same fault in the same wave have spent the last decade moving in opposite directions. One state is building towers. The other one repealed

the law that kept schools and hospitals out of the flood zone in the first place. If you live anywhere on the Washington or Oregon coast, which I've had the pleasure of living near when I was little, do me a favor in the comments.

Tell me whether you know where your nearest high ground is and roughly how long it takes to walk there. Not driving, walking. I'd like to see how many people actually have that number. Also, a thumbs-up on this video goes a
long way. Thank you so much. So, let's start with why vertical evacuation exists at all. The whole idea rests on one uncomfortable fact about the Cascadia coast. In a distant tsunami,
one generated by an earthquake in Alaska or Japan, you'd get hours of warning and a car is useful for you. In a local Cascadia event, the earthquake and the tsunami are the same event. There's no
warning to issue because the ground telling you is the warning. And a lot of the Washington outer coast is a low sand spit surrounded on three sides by water with the nearest natural high ground
several miles inland across bridges that may not survive the shaking. So, if you can't get people out horizontally, the remaining option is to get them up. There's a second piece of this that
locals on the coast are taught and visitors almost never hear about. In a local Cascadia event, no official message will reach you before the water does. The alert systems we have are

built for distant sources where a buoy detects a wave in an open ocean and there's time to push a message out. When the fault under your feet is the source, the shaking is the alert. Strong shaking on the Washington or Oregon coast or
shaking that goes on longer than about 20 seconds means you move immediately on foot toward high ground or designated structure without waiting for any sirens
or phone alert or anybody's permission to do it. It's too late if you wait for confirmation. The confirmation is the water. Back in 2010 and 2011, the University of Washington and the state

emergency management division ran a project called Safe Haven funded through the National Tsunami Hazard Mitigation Program. They worked with three focused communities on the coast and they looked at four different ways of building
height into a flat place. Towers, which are free-standing platforms with stairs or ramps. Burms, which are engineered hills, essentially artificial high ground, and combinations of those two.
And regular buildings designed with a survivable roof on top. So, a school or a fire station or a parking structure does double duty. Communities sat down with maps and worked out where people

actually are during the day and how far each of them could realistically get in 10 minutes. Those reports are still online and the concept drawings in them are worth a look. What I'm looking at here is the burm

option, which is essentially an engineered hill with a path switchbacking up the side of it. That's the one that surprises people because it doesn't read as emergency infrastructure at all. It reads as a park. That work
turned into a design manual. Washington now publishes a document called the Manual for Tsunami Vertical Evacuation Structures, currently in its second edition, and it's the reference
engineers use when they design one of these things. Because a tsunami refuge has to survive two disasters in a row. First, a magnitude 9 earthquake shakes it for 5 minutes, and then minutes
later, a wall of water hits that same structure carrying logs, boats, vehicles, and pieces of other buildings. And it has to stay standing through both of those with hundreds of people already

on the roof. That's a set of loads no ordinary building code contemplates. A normal structural code asks about the snow, wind, and seismic shaking, but a tsunami refuge has to be checked against hydrodynamic force, which is moving
water pushing on a wall, buoyancy, which is water trying to lift the structure, debris impact, a solid object arriving at speed, and debris damming, where a raft of wreckage piles

against the columns and turns a slender frame into a solid wall the flow has to push through. And scour, which is the current excavating the sand out from under the foundation while all of that is happening. The manual is now in its
second edition because the field keeps learning. A great deal of what engineers now know about how buildings behave in a tsunami came from surveying what survived and what didn't in Indonesia in
2004 and in Japan in 2011. That knowledge has been arriving steadily rather than all at once. Okay, now that brings us to the first one ever built. Ocosta Elementary School sits in
Westport, Grays Harbor County. In 2016, it became the first vertical evacuation structure in North America. The refuge is the roof of the school gymnasium, and it's rated for more than
a thousand people. The platform sits at about 55 ft above sea level and roughly 28 ft above the ground it stands on. Ramps and stairways run up the outside, so you don't have to

enter the building to reach the top. The engineering underneath is where it gets really interesting. The foundation uses drilled piles driven around 50 ft down past the soil layers that are expected to liquefy in a long earthquake, and

deep enough that scour doesn't undermine it, too. The main stair towers are reinforced concrete. The columns on the seaward face are encased in concrete so that debris impact, like a shipping container
or a log doing 30 mph, hit something that can absorb that. The whole thing was designed using performance-based methods, meaning the engineers modeled specific hazard

scenarios and check that structure against them, rather than just applying a building code written for ordinary weather. So, the University of Washington tsunami modeling group worked directly with the

design team on the wave loads. But, the part of the Ocosta story that I'm getting to isn't about the engineering. It's the vote to get there. The old school buildings there were nearly a century old and sitting inside
the inundation zone. Replacing them meant a school bond, and a school bond in Washington needs a supermajority. The district put the measure on the ballot, and it failed. They put it up
again, and it failed again. And then, in April of 2013, they went back a third time. The bond was for $13.8 million. It passed with 69.78%
of the vote. 875 people voted yes. Read that number again, because it's the bigger picture in miniature. A small coastal district, twice told no, going
back a third time to ask its neighbors to tax themselves to build a roof their children might have to stand on, and getting a supermajority. Major General Brett Daugherty, who led the state's

military department, and John Schelling, who ran Washington's earthquake and tsunami program at the time, both spoke at the opening. But, the thing worth noticing is that the first tsunami refuge in North
America happened because a school district needed a new school anyway, and someone had the sense to ask what the roof could do. Now, the second one is a different kind of story. The Shoalwater
Bay Indian Tribe lives at Tokeland in Pacific County, on land that's almost entirely inside the inundation zone. The tribe spent years working towards a tsunami refuge and on August 5th, 2022,
they dedicated the first free-standing tsunami evacuation tower in North America. It stands 50 ft tall. There are two decks on it, one at 40 ft and one at 50.

The support piers go 55 ft below ground. It's rated for more than 400 people, which is meaningfully more than the tribal population, and the tribe made it open to anyone in the area during a disaster.

So, good news. If you're a visitor driving through Tokeland when the ground starts moving, that tower is yours as much as it's theirs. The money came together the way that most of these do, in pieces. The tribe continued contributed $1.2
million of its own funds and FEMA provided more than 3 million. The timing at Tokeland is tighter than at Westport in one respect and looser in
another. Modeling suggests the community can reach the tower in 15 to 20 minutes on foot and waves may take around 35 minutes to arrive there. That's a real margin. Small, but real, and it only
exists because the town is close. Chairwoman Charlene Nelson said something at the dedication that I think is really meaningful. She said it could work in any community and that working

together makes such a big difference. Lee Shipman, who worked on the project, put it more directly. She said that they helped change from being helpless victims into knowing that they can survive working together.

And a tribal member named Lynn Clark said simply that the tower will save their lives someday. Robert Ezell, who directs the state's emergency management division, said at the same dedication that they were going to build others up
and down the tsunami hazard zones. Four years on, let's see where that stands today. The third structure is underway right now and it's the first purpose-built public tower in Washington that isn't
attached to a school or a tribe. It's going into the Marina District in Westport. Construction cost is around $11.4 million and the bulk of the money is a $16.7
million FEMA grant awarded in November 2023 under the program then called Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities. Capacity is 2,000 people. Design work
began in 2020 following a planning grant in 2018. The county held a public open house on the design in late May 2026, this year, and construction was scheduled to begin in early August of 2026 with a
completion date of August 31st, 2027. Hannah Cleverly, deputy director of Grays Harbor County Emergency Management, described what the marina
site does in plain terms. She said having a site down in the marina district provides a fighting chance for people to survive when the large Cascadia subduction zone earthquake occurs.

A fighting chance. That's careful language, and it's chosen carefully because the alternative on that spit is nothing at all. The federal funding for that project hit delays and was released in stages, which

is worth flagging because it tells you something about the pace of this work generally. Ocean Shores has also received federal funding toward a possible fourth structure, and the funding pattern is the common obstacle
in all of this. Look at how the three existing projects were paid for, and you get three different answers. Ocosta came from a local school bond, meaning a few thousand coastal residents
taxed themselves. Shoalwater Bay came from tribal funds plus a federal grant. Westport is overwhelmingly a competitive federal award that took 5 years to move

from planning grant to groundbreaking. There's no standing program that simply builds these. Every single one is assembled from scratch by a small local government with a handful of staff competing against every other hazard
project in the country for the same pot of money. Which is why a hazard the state has fully mapped and fully costed still gets addressed at roughly one structure every
3 years. The part I want you to see is the county table, because the county table is the whole argument on one screen. Pacific County came out needing somewhere between 25 and 40 structures.
Grays Harbor County, 30 to 42, and Clallam County, one to three. Add those up, and you get the statewide figure that I mentioned at the start. At least 58, and potentially more than 80. At the
pace of roughly one structure every three years, and at 11 to 14 million dollars each, the math on finishing the job runs into the centuries of years and billions of dollars.
That's the scale of it, and nobody involved says it's otherwise. But, the state is doing something, which is more than most places facing this hazard can say. And it's doing it at a fraction of

the speed that the hazard would justify if money and time were unlimited. Both of those things are true at once. So, that's Washington. Now, cross the Columbia River. Oregon faces the same subduction zone,
the same fault, and the same wave, in many places the same low coastal geography. In 1995, the Oregon legislature passed Senate Bill 379, which did something no other West Coast
state had ever done. It banned the construction of new essential facilities inside the tsunami inundation zone. That's your schools, hospitals, jails,

police, fire stations. The buildings that you would vitally need after a disaster happens, and the buildings full of people who can't evacuate themselves. They were prohibited from being built in the area
the water is expected to reach. And I do have sympathy for the confusion sitting underneath all of this. So, I should tell you where that comes from. I lived in the Pacific Northwest about

from 8 years old to 12 years old. In the Vancouver area, actually. Mount St. Helens was recent enough that the adults in my life talked about it a lot. And one thing about it never made sense to me. If this place was so dangerous
that grown adults still spoke about it that way, why were we all still living here? Nobody ever gave me an answer that I found satisfying. I understand now that there isn't a clean answer. People
live where their work is, where their families are, and the coast is beautiful, and the fault hasn't moved in anybody's lifetime. Every town on both sides of that river is built on that

calculation, and a law telling them that a town can never build another school is arguing with it directly. Scientists who study the fault objected publicly and directly. Their position was that the buildings covered by the ban are
precisely the buildings that shouldn't be there and that removing the prohibition puts people in the water. For context on how unusual either position is, California never had a ban

on this kind of thing at all. So, that's the shape of the last decade on the coast. One state has been slowly and inexpensively building places for people to climb. The other removed the rule that kept its schools out of the water.

Both decisions came from elected people responding to what their constituents told them mattered. And of course, Mother Nature's fault line doesn't know about either one of those positions. I should say that
Oregon hasn't stopped working on tsunami safety. The state's geology agency maintains detailed evacuation mapping. Coastal communities run drills and the repeal removed a prohibition rather than
a preparedness program, right? What it did remove was the one rule that operated on the time scale a subduction earthquake actually runs on. A drill helps the people who are there this
year. But a building lasts 50 to 100 years and where you decide to put it is a decision about people who haven't been born yet. Now, before I shift gears, I want to be careful about a few things

before we get to what you can do. A vertical evacuation structure does one job, right? You climb it, you can survive the tsunami wave. But then, you're standing on a platform in a wrecked landscape waiting for help that

will take days to arrive. Possibly it'll happen in February and possibly in the rain. These towers save you from drowning, but that leaves you with whatever you're carrying when you climb the stairs. That's all you have with
you. Capacity figures are also engineering estimates. They assume people arrive in an orderly way and they stand close together. Reported capacities vary
depending on who's quoting them. In a real event, the number that matters is how many people can physically get there in time. Which unfortunately is usually smaller than the platform will hold.

And there's an unsolved question underneath all this that I don't have a a answer to. Every one of these structures is a decision about who gets covered. Building a tower in the Marina District means the Marina District has a chance. It doesn't help someone 3 miles
up the road. Every sitting choice draws a line on a map and people live on both sides of that. So, the practicality for you and me. The single most useful thing you can do,

if you live on or visit this coast, is find out whether you're inside the inundation zone. Washington's Department of Natural Resources publishes tsunami hazard and evacuation mapping. State Emergency
Management Division hosts the walk time modeling. Oregon's Department of Geology and Mineral Industries publishes equivalent maps for its side of the river. These are public and free and
I'll link them for you in the description. Now, the second thing, and this is the one almost nobody does, is time your own walk. Take the evacuation route from your house or your workplace,
your kids school, and walk it. Not driving it. Walk it at the pace that you would manage if you were maybe frightened, the road surface was broken up. If it takes you 50 minutes, well,

you now know something extremely important about your own situation that no map was going to tell you. Third, if there's a vertical evacuation structure near you, go and look at it in the daylight. Know which stairway you'd use.

Know it well enough that you don't have to think about it so much. And fourth, work out the version of your plan that assumes you're not at home. Most people build their emergency thinking around a kitchen in their garage, and most tsunami deaths on a coast like this one
will be people who are at work, at school, or at the beach, or driving through. If you commute onto the spit or your children are at a school inside the zone, or you visit the coast twice a
year for a weekend, those are separate plans. Each one of them needs its own answer to the same question. From this exact spot on foot, where do I go? How long does it take me to get there? That
question has a different answer at every point on the map. The only way to have it in an emergency is to have worked it out beforehand. If you'd like more of these, subscribing helps that happen.

What I'll promise you in return is that everything on this channel is sourced to the agency that published it, and I'll tell you when two sources disagree instead of picking whichever one sounds better.

And when I realize I get something wrong, I promise I'll correct it. Thanks for watching. If this was worth your time, a like helps it reach the people who live on that coast. I'll see you in the next one.
